rows.speaker: commentators (R, Ṭ, Z)
rows.claim: They commonly distinguish baʾsāʾ as lost wealth and straitened circumstances from ḍarrāʾ as illness and physical suffering.
rows.anchor: Many commentators suggest that the first refers to loss of wealth and straitened circumstances, and the second to illness and physical suffering

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both good and evil test faith: ease can prompt exultation or forgetfulness, while adversity can prompt despair or ingratitude.
rows.anchor: Encounters with both good and evil serve as tests of faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adversity, or alternating hardship and ease, can deepen the spiritual test that comes with a prophet's mission.
rows.anchor: Tests of adversity or ease are sometimes mentioned, as here, in connection with the sending of prophets and messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When people fail to meet adversity with humility, their hearts harden.
rows.anchor: when people fail to respond to such tests of adversity with humility, their hearts are hardened

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan makes evil actions appear good; the Quran also presents this delusion as a general human tendency.
rows.anchor: the Quran also suggests that this delusion is a general human tendency

rows.speaker: commentators (R, Z)
rows.claim: One interpretation is that they forgot the lesson of their hardship: their utter dependence on God.
rows.anchor: they forgot the lesson they should have learned from their misfortune and hardship (R, Z) regarding their utter dependency on God

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that they forgot the messenger's message.
rows.anchor: or they forgot the message brought by the messenger (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God withheld immediate punishment, then removed suffering and granted ease and prosperity by opening everything to them.
rows.anchor: God did not send immediate punishment, but rather opened unto them the gates of all things, removing their suffering and granting them ease and prosperity.

rows.speaker: some commentators (R, Z)
rows.claim: God's alternation of hardship and ease resembles a caring father's discipline, intended to cultivate moral character.
rows.anchor: likened by some to the actions of a caring father, who is by turns harsh and gentle with his child, seeking to cultivate moral character

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, God grants temporary ease to hardened rejectors to lure them further toward the world.
rows.anchor: can be understood as a means by which they are lured further toward the world (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: Abundant worldly provision despite disobedience is a temptation from God.
rows.anchor: given much to one of His servants in this world, despite his disobedience, it is only as a temptation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They exulted, taking prosperity as proof that they were blessed and that their actions were beautiful and good.
rows.anchor: they exulted, thinking they had been blessed and that their actions were therefore fair, in the sense of beautiful and good

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mublisūn conveys regret or being dumbfounded and unable to speak in one's defense.
rows.anchor: which also connotes those in a state of regret or those who are dumbfounded, unable to speak in defense of themselves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mublisūn is said to be related to Iblīs, the Quranic name of Satan.
rows.anchor: It is said to be related to the name Iblīs (Ṭ), a name of Satan in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their despair was sharpened by its contrast with their recent ease and prosperity, as Iblīs's banishment contrasts with his former nearness to God.
rows.anchor: Their sense of despair, when God seized them suddenly, was heightened because of the contrast with the ease and prosperity they had enjoyed previously

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses teach detachment from worldly adversity and prosperity: neither bitterness nor self-satisfaction, since life's turns do not prove God's pleasure or displeasure.
rows.anchor: the vicissitudes of earthly life are merely a Divine test and do not necessarily reflect either Divine pleasure or dissatisfaction.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cutting off a people's last remnant means uprooting and eliminating them entirely, here through sudden punishment such as that in verse 44.
rows.anchor: means to “uproot” and eliminate them entirely as a people, in this case through a sudden punishment, such as that mentioned in v. 44

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is followed by praise recognizing God's many merciful efforts to guide the people before their destruction.
rows.anchor: in recognition of God’s many merciful efforts to bring these people to guidance before their destruction (R, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly presents worship of idols and false deities that neither benefit nor harm as folly.
rows.anchor: The folly of worshipping that which neither benefits nor harms is repeatedly mentioned in relation to idols and false deities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling on anything besides God for help is futile, as illustrated by Quranic parables.
rows.anchor: The futility of “calling upon” any other than God for help is evoked in 2:171

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning back on one's heels means returning to ignorance after receiving God's guidance.
rows.anchor: To “turn back on one’s heels” means to return to a state of ignorance after having received God’s guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satans in the plural and general sense are agents of Satan, including jinn and human beings who knowingly or unknowingly do his bidding.
rows.anchor: Satans, in the plural and general form, refers to the agents of Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both human and jinn satans seduce people through whispering, subtly drawing them away from guidance.
rows.anchor: are said to “seduce” human beings through “whispering,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran's account of satans serving Solomon suggests that in some passages the term simply means jinn.
rows.anchor: satans in the service of the prophet Solomon (21:82; 38:37), suggesting that in some places they simply refer to jinn.

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī figuratively reads being seduced on earth as being lured into a deep hole.
rows.anchor: as read figuratively by al-Rāzī, “lure them into a deep hole.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companions calling the bewildered person to guidance can mean sincere, rightly guided people whose appeal goes unheeded.
rows.anchor: referring to sincere and rightly guided companions who try to persuade him to follow guidance, but their call goes unheeded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If verse 70 concerns Abū Bakr's son luring his father to idolatry, this verse may depict Abū Bakr calling his son to guidance.
rows.anchor: If v. 70 was revealed in relation to the attempt of Abū Bakr’s son to lure his father to idolatry

rows.speaker: a minority of commentators (R, Ṭ)
rows.claim: A minority interpret the companions' call as an invitation to false guidance.
rows.anchor: A minority, however, interpret the guidance to which the companions call to be false guidance (R, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's guidance is the only true guidance; any other path called guidance leads astray.
rows.anchor: there is no guidance outside of His; all paths to which one may be “guided,” other than His, are paths that lead astray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet answers idolatrous calls by affirming submission to the Lord of the worlds, canonical prayer five times daily, and reverence as mindfulness of God's presence, commands, and prohibitions.
rows.anchor: to perform the prayer—that is, the canonical prayer, performed five times a day

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī maps submission to the best act of the heart, prayer to the best act of the limbs, and reverence to the best act of omission because it helps avoid sin.
rows.anchor: prayer is the best of the acts of the limbs; and reverence is the best of the “acts of omission,”

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Some relatives among the forefathers, descendants, and brothers were chosen and guided, but not all; some became disbelievers.
rows.anchor: some from among their fathers, and their progeny, and their brethren were “chosen” and guided, but not all

rows.speaker: commentators (Ṭ)
rows.claim: Being chosen may mean being selected for God's religion or to bring His messages to people.
rows.anchor: chosen for God’s religion or chosen to bring His messages to people

rows.speaker: commentators (Ṭ)
rows.claim: Alternatively, being chosen may mean God singled them out for His love.
rows.anchor: it could also mean that God singled them out for His Love (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to say that he seeks no monetary or other reward for his message, as do several other messengers.
rows.anchor: he seeks no reward, monetary or other, for the message he brings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder for all worlds is the Quran, whose message is universal rather than limited to one people.
rows.anchor: The reminder for the worlds (cf. 12:104; 38:87; 68:52; 81:27) is the Quran, a description or title indicating that the relevance of its message is universal

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some interpret the rule as requiring invocation of God's Name over every kind of food.
rows.anchor: a condition for all kinds of food that one would eat (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: For meat, the rule forbids carrion because God's Name was not invoked over the animal before it died.
rows.anchor: in the case of meat would forbid the eating of carrion, since God’s Name would not have been invoked over it before it died

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A debate about eating carrion is reported as the occasion for the revelation of verses 116–117.
rows.anchor: where a debate over the eating of carrion is reported to be the reason for the revelation of the verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Invoking God's Name and slaughtering animals ritually makes their meat permissible for Muslims.
rows.anchor: Both the invocation of God’s Name over the animals to be slaughtered and the ritual manner of slaughtering them make the meat ḥalāl

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other dietary laws prohibit carrion while allowing normally unlawful food in cases of necessity caused by hunger.
rows.anchor: where, as here, an exception is made for those who are compelled by necessity

rows.speaker: commentators (Ṭ)
rows.claim: Some commentators take God's having expounded the forbidden to refer to the more detailed dietary laws revealed later in Medina, although this verse came earlier in Mecca.
rows.anchor: refers to the more detailed dietary laws as found in 5:3–5 (Ṭ), although these detailed laws were revealed in Madinah, while the present verse was revealed earlier in Makkah

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī suggests that, given the later timing of the full dietary laws, the phrase could mean God “will expound” the forbidden rules.
rows.anchor: al-Qurṭubī suggests the possibility that He has expounded for you that which He has forbidden should be understood to mean, “He will expound for you.”

rows.speaker: some commentators (Q)
rows.claim: Those led astray by caprice may be people arguing that carrion killed by God is preferable to meat slaughtered by human hands.
rows.anchor: better to eat carrion (which was, in a sense, killed by God), than to eat what their own hands had slaughtered (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They lead people astray through caprice and ignorance because their case rests on conjecture and surmise.
rows.anchor: since their arguments are based upon conjecture and surmise (see v. 116).

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: The general reading forbids eating any food without God's Name, including meat sacrificed to false gods or under pagan rites and carrion.
rows.anchor: believers should not eat any food (meat or otherwise) over which the Name of God has not been invoked

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meat slaughtered by Muslims who merely neglect or forget the invocation is generally considered licit.
rows.anchor: the meat of animals slaughtered by Muslims who simply neglect or forget to invoke God’s Name during the slaughtering is generally considered licit to consume

rows.speaker: Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī
rows.claim: They allow meat when God's Name was omitted during Muslim slaughter, whether the omission was inadvertent or deliberate.
rows.anchor: Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī considered it legitimate to consume such meat whether the omission of God’s Name was inadvertent or deliberate

rows.speaker: Abū Ḥanīfah and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal
rows.claim: They disallow meat if a Muslim deliberately omitted God's Name during slaughter.
rows.anchor: held that if the omission was deliberate, one should not eat the meat (Q, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse likely continues the response to idolaters who argued carrion had been “slaughtered by God” despite human agency.
rows.anchor: that carrion is meat that has been ultimately “slaughtered by God,”

rows.speaker: some accounts (W)
rows.claim: Some accounts say the carrion argument persuaded some Companions, prompting this verse to clarify that eating without God's Name is sin and disobedience.
rows.anchor: the idolaters’ argument appeared persuasive to some of the Prophet’s Companions (W)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this context, iniquity means clear sin and disobedience.
rows.anchor: eating that over which the Name of God has not been invoked is iniquity, that is, a clear sin and an act of disobedience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The satans who inspire disputation may be human beings or jinn.
rows.anchor: the satans, who may here be human beings or jinn

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: A general reading is that people engaged in disingenuous debate over God's law encourage one another in their disputations.
rows.anchor: those who engage in such disingenuous debate concerning God’s Law encourage and incite one another in their disputations (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: some reports (Ṭ, W)
rows.claim: Some reports identify the disputing satans as Persian Zoroastrians allied with Quraysh, who devised the carrion argument and urged idolaters to use it.
rows.anchor: certain Persian Zoroastrians, allied with the Quraysh, who formulated the argument regarding carrion mentioned above and encouraged the idolaters to use it against the Prophet

rows.speaker: some reports (Q, Ṭ)
rows.claim: Other reports say the verse concerned Jews who argued with the Prophet about eating carrion.
rows.anchor: the verse concerned a group of Jews who similarly argued with the Prophet on the issue of eating carrion (Q, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators adopt the general interpretation of the verse rather than the specific Zoroastrian or Jewish identifications.
rows.anchor: Most commentators, however, subscribed to the more general interpretation of the verse mentioned above.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse links the straight path, upright religion, Abraham's creed, being ḥanīf, and rejection of idolatry, concepts that recur together in the Quran.
rows.anchor: This verse mentions together the concepts of a straight path, upright religion, the creed of Abraham, the religious description ḥanīf, and the shunning of idolatry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path denotes true religion leading to felicity in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: the path of true religion that leads to felicity in this life and the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also refers to upright religion in other passages.
rows.anchor: For other references to upright religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Millah, translated “creed,” can mean a religious community or its particular belief system.
rows.anchor: Creed here translates millah, which sometimes denotes a religious community, but can also refer to its particular belief system or creed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanīf is usually associated with Abraham in the Quran.
rows.anchor: The description ḥanīf is usually mentioned in connection with Abraham in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some verses directly call the Prophet and his community to be ḥanīf.
rows.anchor: although in some verses the Prophet Muhammad and his community are called upon directly to be ḥanīf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic tradition commonly uses ḥanīf to describe Muhammad's religious life and practice before prophethood.
rows.anchor: Islamic tradition commonly uses this term to describe Muhammad’s religious life and practice even before his call to prophethood.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In some contexts ḥanīf is distinguished from Judaism and Christianity, while the Quran also says Jews and Christians were called to be ḥanīf.
rows.anchor: the Quran indicates that Jews and Christians were also called to be
